title: Preteritum / Simple Past Tense
bridge: In Norwegian, the simple past tense (preteritum) is formed differently than in English. Regular verbs add an '-et' or '-te' ending, while irregular verbs have unique forms. Unlike English, Norwegian does not use auxiliary verbs like 'did' for negation or questions in the past tense. Be cautious with irregular verbs, as they don't follow a consistent pattern, similar to English irregular verbs like 'go' and 'went'.
rule: For regular verbs in Norwegian, the simple past tense is formed by adding '-et' or '-te' to the verb stem. For example, 'snakke' (to speak) becomes 'snakket'. Irregular verbs have their own past tense forms, such as 'gå' (to go) becoming 'gikk'. The past tense is used to describe completed actions in the past. Negation is formed by adding 'ikke' after the verb, e.g., 'Jeg snakket ikke' (I did not speak). Questions follow the same structure as statements, without auxiliary verbs.

common_error.explanation: English speakers often transfer the use of 'did' for negation in the past tense. In Norwegian, simply add 'ikke' after the verb without using an auxiliary verb.

title: Presens progresiv / Present Progressive
bridge: In Norwegian, the present progressive (presens progresiv) is similar to English in that it describes actions happening now. However, Norwegian uses the verb 'å være' (to be) + the present participle (ending in -ende), whereas English uses 'to be' + the -ing form. A key difference is that Norwegian often omits the subject pronoun, unlike English. Be careful not to overuse the present progressive in Norwegian, as it is less common than in English for ongoing actions.
rule: The present progressive in Norwegian is formed with the verb 'å være' (to be) in the present tense, followed by the present participle of the main verb (ending in -ende). The present participle is the same for all subjects. Common uses include describing actions happening at the moment of speaking or temporary situations. Note that Norwegian often prefers the simple present for ongoing actions, unlike English.

title: Futuro con 'kommer til å' / Future with 'going to'
bridge: In Norwegian, the equivalent of the English 'going to' future is 'kommer til å'. Unlike English, where 'going to' is used for both plans and predictions, Norwegian often uses 'kommer til å' for intentions and 'vil' for predictions. Be careful not to directly translate 'going to' as 'gå til' in this context, as it would be incorrect.
rule: To express the future in Norwegian using 'kommer til å', place 'kommer til å' before the infinitive verb. This structure is used to talk about plans or intentions. For example: 'Jeg kommer til å reise' (I am going to travel). Note that the verb following 'kommer til å' remains in its infinitive form, unlike in English where the verb is in the base form after 'going to'.

title: Futuro simple / Simple Future
bridge: In Norwegian, the simple future is often expressed using the verb 'å bli' (to become) followed by a verb in the infinitive form, which is different from English where 'will' is commonly used. For example, 'I will go' in Norwegian is 'Jeg skal gå'. Be careful not to directly translate 'will' as it can lead to incorrect sentences. Additionally, Norwegian also uses 'å komme til å' (to come to) for a more distant or certain future action, similar to 'going to' in English.
rule: The simple future in Norwegian can be formed in two main ways: 1) Using 'skal' + infinitive verb (e.g., 'Jeg skal spise' - I will eat) for intentions or plans. 2) Using 'komme til å' + infinitive verb (e.g., 'Jeg kommer til å reise' - I will travel) for more certain or distant future actions. Note that 'skal' is more common in everyday speech. There are no irregular forms, and the structure remains the same for all subjects.

title: Sammenligninger og superlativer / Comparatives and Superlatives
bridge: In Norwegian, comparatives and superlatives are formed differently than in English. While English often adds '-er' or '-est' to adjectives, Norwegian typically uses 'mere' (more) and 'mest' (most) for comparatives and superlatives, respectively. Be cautious with irregular adjectives like 'god' (good), which becomes 'bedre' (better) and 'best' (best), similar to English but with distinct forms.
rule: For most adjectives, use 'mere' for comparatives and 'mest' for superlatives. Example: 'stor' (big) → 'mere stor' (bigger) → 'mest stor' (biggest). Irregular adjectives have specific forms, e.g., 'god' → 'bedre' → 'best'. Superlatives often add 'den' (the) before the adjective, e.g., 'den største' (the biggest).

title: Modale verb / Modal Verbs
bridge: In Norwegian, modal verbs like 'skal', 'kan', and 'må' express necessity, possibility, and obligation, similar to English 'should', 'can', and 'must'. However, Norwegian modals often appear in their base form regardless of the subject, unlike English where they change (e.g., 'I can' vs. 'he can'). Be cautious with 'skal', which can imply a stronger obligation than 'should' in some contexts.
rule: Modal verbs in Norwegian are used to express necessity, possibility, or obligation. The main modals are 'skal' (must/shall), 'kan' (can), 'må' (must/may), and 'vil' (will). Unlike English, Norwegian modals do not change form based on the subject. They are followed by the infinitive form of the verb. For example, 'Jeg skal gå' (I must go) and 'Han kan snakke' (He can speak). 'Skal' often implies a stronger obligation than 'should', while 'må' can express both necessity and permission.

title: Refleksive verb / Reflexive Verbs
bridge: In Norwegian, reflexive verbs are used similarly to English, but with a key difference: the reflexive pronoun always matches the subject in person and number. Unlike English, where 'myself' can be used for both 'I' and 'me', Norwegian uses 'meg' for 'meg' and 'deg' for 'deg'. Be careful not to omit the reflexive pronoun, as it is required in Norwegian even when it might be optional in English.
rule: Reflexive verbs in Norwegian are used when the subject and object of the verb are the same. The reflexive pronoun agrees with the subject in person and number. Common reflexive pronouns are: meg (myself), deg (yourself), seg (himself/herself/itself/themselves). Reflexive verbs often involve actions done to oneself. Examples include 'å vaske seg' (to wash oneself) and 'å klippe seg' (to cut oneself).

title: Pronomene for direkte og indirekte objekt / Direct and Indirect Object Pronouns
bridge: In Norwegian, object pronouns are similar to English, but their placement is more flexible. Unlike English, Norwegian object pronouns can appear before or after the verb, depending on emphasis. Additionally, Norwegian has a distinct set of pronouns for indirect objects, which are less common in English. Be cautious not to confuse direct and indirect object pronouns, as their forms differ slightly.
rule: Norwegian object pronouns replace noun objects to avoid repetition. Direct object pronouns (meg, deg, seg, oss, dere, seg) refer to the receiver of the action, while indirect object pronouns (meg, deg, ham, henne, oss, dere, seg) indicate to whom or for whom the action is performed. Pronouns can precede or follow the verb, with post-verbal placement being more common in neutral sentences. Note that 'seg' is reflexive and used when the object is the same as the subject.

common_error.explanation: English speakers often redundantly add possessive pronouns (e.g., 'hans') after using an object pronoun. In Norwegian, the object pronoun ('ham') already indicates the recipient, so adding 'hans' is unnecessary and incorrect.

title: Adverbios de frecuencia / Frequency Adverbs
bridge: In Norwegian, frequency adverbs like 'alltid' (always), 'ofte' (often), and 'aldri' (never) are placed after the verb in the main clause, unlike in English where they typically appear before the verb. Be careful not to place them at the beginning of the sentence, as this can change the emphasis and sound unnatural in Norwegian. Also, note that Norwegian frequency adverbs do not change form, regardless of the subject or tense.
rule: Frequency adverbs in Norwegian are used to indicate how often an action occurs. They are placed immediately after the verb in the main clause. Common adverbs include 'alltid' (always), 'ofte' (often), 'som regel' (usually), 'sjelden' (rarely), and 'aldri' (never). These adverbs do not change form and are used consistently across tenses and subjects. In questions, the adverb remains after the verb, even if the word order changes.

title: Preposisjoner for tid / Prepositions of Time
bridge: In Norwegian, prepositions of time like 'på', 'i', and 'om' are used differently than their English counterparts 'on', 'in', and 'at'. For instance, 'på' is used for days and dates, while 'i' is for months and years, contrasting with English where 'on' is used for both days and dates. Be cautious with 'om', which means 'in' or 'after' a period of time, but is not interchangeable with English 'about'.
rule: Use 'på' for specific days and dates (e.g., 'på mandag', 'på 17. mai'). Use 'i' for months, seasons, and years (e.g., 'i januar', 'i vinter', 'i 2023'). Use 'om' to express time in the future (e.g., 'om tre dager' means 'in three days'). Note that 'klokken' is used for specific times (e.g., 'klokken 8').

common_error.explanation: English speakers often incorrectly use 'på' before days of the week. In Norwegian, 'på' is used with 'mandag' but not required for other days when specifying an activity. Simply say 'Jeg møter tirsdag' instead of 'Jeg møter på tirsdag'.

title: Sammenhengsord / Conjunctions
bridge: In Norwegian, conjunctions like 'og' (and), 'men' (but), and 'fordi' (because) function similarly to their English counterparts, but word order can be more flexible. For instance, 'fordi' often appears at the beginning of a sentence, which is less common in English. Be cautious with 'ellers' (or), as it can imply a stronger consequence than 'or' in English.
rule: Conjunctions in Norwegian connect words, phrases, or clauses. Common ones include 'og' (and), 'men' (but), 'eller' (or), 'fordi' (because), 'når' (when), and 'hvis' (if). Word order is generally flexible, but the conjunction typically precedes the second clause. 'Fordi' often starts a sentence, and 'ellers' can imply a stronger alternative or consequence.

title: Perfekt / Present Perfect
bridge: In Norwegian, the present perfect (perfekt) is similar to English in that it describes actions completed in the past with a result in the present. However, Norwegian uses the auxiliary verb 'ha' (to have) more consistently than English, which often uses 'have' but sometimes 'be' for certain verbs. Additionally, Norwegian doesn’t use the auxiliary verb for emphasis or in short answers, unlike English.
rule: The Norwegian present perfect (perfekt) is formed with the auxiliary verb 'ha' (to have) in the present tense + the past participle of the main verb. The past participle is formed by adding '-et' or '-d' to the verb stem for regular verbs. Irregular verbs have unique past participle forms. Use this tense to describe completed actions with present relevance, similar to English. Note: Norwegian does not use the auxiliary verb in short answers or for emphasis, unlike English.

common_error.explanation: English speakers often incorrectly use the past tense (e.g., 'gått') instead of the present perfect for actions completed in the past with present relevance. In Norwegian, the present perfect is the correct choice here, but the error lies in assuming 'gått' is wrong—it’s actually correct. The mistake is in thinking Norwegian always mirrors English tense usage.

title: Imperativ / Imperative
bridge: In Norwegian, the imperative form is often the same as the infinitive form of the verb, similar to English. However, Norwegian does not use the subject pronoun 'you' in imperative sentences, unlike English where it is often included for clarity. Be cautious with negative imperatives, as Norwegian uses a different structure than English, which typically adds 'don't' before the verb.
rule: The affirmative imperative in Norwegian is formed by using the infinitive form of the verb. For negative imperatives, use 'ikke' after the verb. Unlike English, Norwegian does not use a separate auxiliary verb like 'do' in negative imperatives. The structure is: Verb + ikke. Remember, the subject pronoun is usually omitted in both affirmative and negative imperatives.

common_error.explanation: English speakers often place 'ikke' before the verb in negative imperatives, following the English structure with 'don't'. In Norwegian, 'ikke' must come after the verb in imperative sentences.

title: Sustantivos contables e incontables / Count and Uncount Nouns
bridge: In Norwegian, countable nouns (like 'bok' - book) can be singular or plural, similar to English. However, uncountable nouns (like 'informasjon' - information) always stay singular, which is different from English where some uncountable nouns can take a plural form in specific contexts (e.g., 'informations'). Additionally, Norwegian uses the same form for singular and plural with uncountable nouns, whereas English often adds 's' or 'es' for plurals.
rule: Countable nouns in Norwegian can be singular or plural, and they often change form in the plural (e.g., 'bok' becomes 'bøker'). Uncountable nouns, however, remain singular and do not change form. They refer to things that cannot be counted individually, such as abstract concepts or substances. When using uncountable nouns, avoid adding 'et' (a/an) or 'en' (a/an) in the plural form, as this is incorrect in Norwegian.

common_error.explanation: English speakers often mistakenly add an 's' to uncountable nouns in Norwegian, thinking it pluralizes them. However, uncountable nouns in Norwegian do not change form in the plural and remain singular. Adding 's' is incorrect and should be avoided.

examples.note: Use 'en' for masculine nouns like 'bil'.

title: Noen og noe / Some and Any
bridge: In Norwegian, 'some' and 'any' are translated as 'noen' and 'noe' respectively, but their usage differs slightly from English. 'Noen' is used for countable nouns, while 'noe' is used for uncountable nouns, similar to English. However, Norwegian often omits these words in affirmative sentences, which can be a trap for English speakers. Additionally, 'noen' can also mean 'someone' or 'some people', adding a layer of complexity.
rule: In Norwegian, 'noen' is used with countable nouns in the plural form, while 'noe' is used with uncountable nouns. For example, 'noen bøker' (some books) and 'noe vann' (some water). In questions and negative sentences, 'noen' and 'noe' are used similarly to English 'some' and 'any'. However, in affirmative sentences, Norwegians often omit these words, saying 'Jeg har bøker' (I have books) instead of 'Jeg har noen bøker' (I have some books). Note that 'noen' can also refer to 'someone' or 'some people', so context is crucial.

concept_examples.text: Vi så noen mennesker i parken.
concept_examples.translation: We saw some people in the park.

common_error.explanation: English speakers often mistakenly use 'noe' with countable nouns, as in 'Jeg har noe bøker'. The correct form is 'Jeg har noen bøker' or simply 'Jeg har bøker', as Norwegians frequently omit 'noen' in affirmative sentences. Remember, 'noe' is only used with uncountable nouns.

examples.note: Use 'noen' with plural countable nouns.

title: Mye, mange, mye av / Much, Many, A Lot Of
bridge: In Norwegian, quantifiers like 'mye' (much) and 'mange' (many) are used similarly to English, but with key differences. 'Mye' is used for uncountable nouns, while 'mange' is for plural countable nouns. Unlike English, Norwegian does not use 'a lot of' directly; instead, 'mye av' is used for uncountable nouns, and 'mange av' for countable nouns. Be careful not to mix 'mye' with 'mange' when referring to countable items.
rule: Use 'mye' for uncountable nouns (e.g., water, love) and 'mange' for plural countable nouns (e.g., books, people). For more specific quantification, use 'mye av' for uncountable nouns and 'mange av' for countable nouns. Note that 'mye' and 'mange' do not change form, regardless of the noun they modify. Always match the quantifier with the correct type of noun.

title: Relativsetninger / Relative Clauses
bridge: In Norwegian, relative clauses are similar to English in structure, using words like 'som' (that/which) to connect information. However, Norwegian often omits the relative pronoun when it’s not the subject, unlike English, which typically retains 'that' or 'which.' Also, word order in Norwegian relative clauses is more flexible, with the verb often appearing at the end of the clause, unlike English’s fixed subject-verb order.
rule: Relative clauses in Norwegian provide additional information about a noun. The relative pronoun 'som' is used for all genders and numbers, equivalent to 'who,' 'which,' or 'that' in English. If 'som' is not the subject of the clause, it can often be omitted. The verb in the relative clause typically appears at the end, following the object. For example: 'Boka som jeg leste var god' (The book that I read was good).
